summary.title: Achieving Non-Inclusive Cache Performance with Inclusive Caches
summary.one_liner: Inclusive last-level caches lose performance mainly through inclusion victims, and Temporal Locality Aware policies (TLH, ECI, QBS) can close most of the gap to non-inclusive caches without extra hardware.
takeaways: Inclusion victims, lines evicted from core caches to maintain inclusion, cause most of the performance loss of inclusive LLCs, more than duplicated capacity.
The LLC replacement state goes stale because core-cache hits are hidden from it, so hot lines decay to LRU and get evicted.
Temporal Locality Hints send LLC updates on every core-cache hit: best results but high traffic, so it is used as a limit study.
Early Core Invalidation evicts the next LRU line from core caches early and relies on a re-request to learn it is hot; it is time sensitive.
Query Based Selection asks core caches whether a candidate victim is resident before evicting it; it performs similarly to a non-inclusive hierarchy without extra hardware structures.
summary.summary: The paper argues that the performance gap of inclusive last-level caches comes mainly from inclusion victims, caused by the LLC not seeing temporal locality in the core caches, rather than from duplicated capacity. It motivates the problem with a reference-pattern example and compares inclusive, non-inclusive and exclusive hierarchies across core-to-LLC size ratios. It then proposes three Temporal Locality Aware policies: TLH (hints on core hits), ECI (early invalidation of the next victim), and QBS (querying core caches before eviction). The evaluation on 2-, 4- and 8-core CMPs reports that all three improve inclusive performance and QBS approaches non-inclusive performance.
